classification_signals: This paper argues for a basic need for graspable 'handles' to be physically present, or merely suggested in our immediate environment. Yet two of the most characteristic elements of industrial-modernist architecture, plate-glass curtain walls and minimalist surfaces, fail to match this aspect of our body's biology. The absence of graspable components from the formal architecture of the 20th Century leads to psychological disconnection on the part of the user, and could possibly be a cause for stress and anxiety. Physical built elements and designs suggestive of grasping arise in traditional and vernacular methods of construction as ubiquitous moldings, ornament, and trim in response to both human psychology and tectonics. (Abstract, p. 1)
The present paper is devoted to outlining the prehensile aspect of object affordance. (p. 2)
I propose several factors that, in the context of design, affect the intensity of this physiological and psychological object affordance effect positively or negatively. (p. 2)

The topic of affordances goes back to 19th Century theories of 'empathy aesthetics'... Later, in the field of psychology, James J. Gibson formulated his theory of affordances (Gibson 1979). Gibson's work initiated a research program that continues to this day, but which has yet to influence architectural design. (p. 6)
A new, adaptive approach to architecture and design pays close attention to human evolution. (p. 6)
The paper does not present new empirical data, methods, or results from an original experiment conducted by the authors.
title: WHY WE NEED TO “GRASP” OUR SURROUNDINGS: OBJECT AFFORDANCE AND PREHENSION IN ARCHITECTURE

findings.antecedent: absence of graspable components from formal architecture (e.g., plate-glass curtain walls, minimalist surfaces)
findings.consequent: psychological disconnection, stress, anxiety
findings.source: Abstract, p. 1
findings.quote: The absence of graspable components from the formal architecture of the 20th Century leads to psychological disconnection on the part of the user, and could possibly be a cause for stress and anxiety.

findings.antecedent: physical built elements and designs suggestive of grasping (e.g., moldings, ornament, trim)
findings.consequent: response to human psychology and tectonics
findings.source: Abstract, p. 1
findings.quote: Physical built elements and designs suggestive of grasping arise in traditional and vernacular methods of construction as ubiquitous moldings, ornament, and trim in response to both human psychology and tectonics.

findings.antecedent: prioritizing human neurological responses in what architects build
findings.consequent: human wellbeing
findings.source: Introduction, p. 1
findings.quote: A quiet revolution is underway, in which architects are beginning to prioritize human neurological responses in what they build... Our state of wellbeing is due in part to largely subconscious effects that environmental information triggers in our body...

findings.antecedent: geometrical configurations adaptive to our body
findings.consequent: innate neurophysiologic mechanisms (instinctive attachment to environment)
findings.source: Different affordance mechanisms cooperate, p. 1
findings.quote: Innate neurophysiologic mechanisms inherited from our evolutionary past attach us to our environment instinctively... Geometrical configurations adaptive to our body may be discovered and catalogued...

findings.antecedent: Biophilia (including nature/plants in living environments, coding biological forms into artificial built environment)
findings.consequent: unselfconscious connection to the healing geometry of our surroundings
findings.source: Different affordance mechanisms cooperate, p. 2
findings.quote: Biophilia triggers unselfconscious connection to the healing geometry of our surroundings, if any is indeed present. Biophilic design tries to apply rules of biological structure to the built environment.

findings.antecedent: fractal scaling (in traditional/vernacular architectures, plant structure, weathering)
findings.consequent: subconscious connection to natural elements
findings.source: Different affordance mechanisms cooperate, p. 2
findings.quote: The user then subconsciously connects to natural elements such as plants and surfaces built from wood or textured stone, etc., and to the mathematics of fractal scaling found in traditional and vernacular architectures.

findings.antecedent: satisfying the sense of prehension (grasping objects with hands)
findings.consequent: kinesthetic anchoring to the environment and situatedness
findings.source: Different affordance mechanisms cooperate, p. 2
findings.quote: Another, distinct connective mechanism independent of biophilia has to do with satisfying the sense of prehension, or grasping objects with our hands... Prehension enables kinesthetic anchoring to the environment, an essential component of our need to be situated in the world.

findings.antecedent: graspable item of a size to fit the average human hand (2-8 cm / 1-3 inches)
findings.consequent: perception of environment as accommodating and providing ready physical 'support'
findings.source: Five architectural characteristics of object affordance (i) SIZE, p. 2
findings.quote: A graspable item of a size to fit the average human hand helps us to perceive an environment as accommodating. It provides ready physical “support" should we ever need it.

findings.antecedent: shape of physically-graspable structural elements that invite comfortable hand contact (prehension), especially smooth, rounded edges
findings.consequent: satisfaction of interest and comfortable/good touch
findings.source: Five architectural characteristics of object affordance (ii) SHAPE, p. 2
findings.quote: The shape of physically-graspable structural elements in a room should invite comfortable hand contact (prehension), even if it never actually occurs. A shape is more likely to satisfy our interest if it offers smooth, rounded edges that will feel comfortable and good to the touch.

findings.antecedent: graspable elements or objects made of transparent, random, or amorphous materials
findings.consequent: invitation to grasping and visibility to object affordance mechanism
findings.source: Five architectural characteristics of object affordance (iii) MATERIAL, p. 2
findings.quote: Graspable elements or objects in a room that are made of transparent, random, or amorphous materials do not invite grasping. They are not defined strongly enough; they remain invisible to the mechanism of object affordance, hence the allure of prehension never occurs.

findings.antecedent: sharp, spiky, angular, rough, or visually unsettling objects (even if correct size and reach)
findings.consequent: signal of possible pain/injury when grasped, repulsion instead of positive connection
findings.source: Five architectural characteristics of object affordance (iv) TEXTURE, p. 2
findings.quote: Sharp, spiky, angular, rough, or otherwise visually unsettling objects, even if they are of the correct size and are situated within easy reach, signal possible pain or injury when grasped. Those repel instead of connecting positively.

findings.antecedent: easily-reachable elements with graspable shapes and designs
findings.consequent: object affordance effect
findings.source: Five architectural characteristics of object affordance (v) DISTANCE, p. 2
findings.quote: The object affordance effect is strongest for easily-reachable elements, and weakest for graspable elements that are situated outside our physical reach. It diminishes with distance.

findings.antecedent: motor neurons continuously perceiving articulations and suggestive designs in immediate surroundings
findings.consequent: subconscious object affordance action to situate people in space
findings.source: Object affordance acts subconsciously on people to situate them in space, hence in the world, p. 3
findings.quote: Object affordance acts subconsciously on people to situate them in space, hence in the world. Our motor neurons continuously perceive articulations and suggestive designs in our immediate surroundings...

findings.antecedent: positive prehensile reaction (triggered by object affordance)
findings.consequent: person's wellbeing and performance
findings.source: Object affordance acts subconsciously on people to situate them in space, hence in the world, p. 3
findings.quote: A positive prehensile reaction enhances a person's wellbeing and performance, whereas a negative affordance set off by structural details that isolate us will influence all other actions negatively through superimposed anxiety and fatigue.

findings.antecedent: negative affordance (set off by structural details that isolate users)
findings.consequent: superimposed anxiety and fatigue, negative influence on actions
findings.source: Object affordance acts subconsciously on people to situate them in space, hence in the world, p. 3
findings.quote: A positive prehensile reaction enhances a person's wellbeing and performance, whereas a negative affordance set off by structural details that isolate us will influence all other actions negatively through superimposed anxiety and fatigue.

findings.antecedent: design components corresponding to bodily dimensions (1mm to 2m)
findings.consequent: major supportive role in using buildings/urban spaces and shaping experience of the whole
findings.source: Scale dependence of space on small things, p. 3
findings.quote: Design components that correspond to bodily dimensions... play a major supportive role in how we use buildings and urban spaces. The existence and organization of ordered structure on these physical human scales shapes our experience of the whole...

findings.antecedent: absence of smaller and intermediate scales in design
findings.consequent: geometrical coherence and situatedness
findings.source: Scale dependence of space on small things, p. 3
findings.quote: Without smaller and intermediate scales, geometrical coherence and situatedness are impossible.

findings.antecedent: full spectrum of human scales in architecture (1mm to 2m)
findings.consequent: positive neurophysiologic interaction with surroundings
findings.source: Scale dependence of space on small things, p. 3
findings.quote: A positive neurophysiologic interaction with our surroundings demands the full spectrum of human scales in architecture...

findings.antecedent: smallest structural scales from 1 mm up to 2 cm (1/16 to 1 inch)
findings.consequent: presence when using natural materials
findings.source: Scale dependence of space on small things, p. 3
findings.quote: The smallest structural scales from 1 mm up to 2 cm (1/16 to 1 inch) are very often present when we decide to (and can afford to) use natural materials.

findings.antecedent: graspable dimensions (1 to 3 inches)
findings.consequent: built and defined on purpose (to profit from object affordance)
findings.source: Scale dependence of space on small things, p. 3
findings.quote: Materials do not normally show graspable dimensions (1 to 3 inches); therefore, to profit from object affordance, those scales need to be built and defined on purpose.

findings.antecedent: tectonic elements smaller than human body size (e.g., frames, trim, moldings, baseboards)
findings.consequent: definition of an enveloping space where one feels psychologically situated
findings.source: Scale dependence of space on small things, p. 3
findings.quote: User wellbeing is linked to all the tectonic elements smaller in size than the human body cooperating to define an enveloping space in which one feels situated psychologically.

findings.antecedent: geometrical coherence in small and intermediate size structural elements
findings.consequent: healing response
findings.source: Scale dependence of space on small things, p. 3
findings.quote: Our brain perceives the small and intermediate size structural elements together as either being coherent (when we perceive a “whole”), or not (when we perceive randomness). Architects wishing to create the healing response triggered by geometrical coherence have to apply specific design techniques.

findings.antecedent: elimination of frames, trim, moldings, baseboards (minimalist modernism)
findings.consequent: anchoring of large-scale spatial form within cognitive system
findings.source: Scale dependence of space on small things, p. 3
findings.quote: Frames, trim, moldings, baseboards – all traditionally ornamental tectonic elements in a building that were eliminated in pursuing a minimalistic modernism are now encouraged to come back... because they are needed to anchor the large-scale spatial form within our cognitive system.

findings.antecedent: oversimplified environments (bereft of graspable subdivisions and designs)
findings.consequent: frustration of object affordance mechanism, diminished/eliminated prehensile connection
findings.source: Minimalist environments are created not to adapt, p. 3-4
findings.quote: Oversimplified environments are intentionally bereft of graspable subdivisions and designs. Structurally necessary frames and supports in such designed spaces that could have satisfied real or virtual prehension are hidden. 'Graspable' handles are generally missing, or in many cases made either too small or too large to grasp, as an intentionality of this peculiar design aesthetic. A minimalist approach to design frustrates the object affordance mechanism, diminishing or eliminating any prehensile connection with our surroundings.

findings.antecedent: elimination of human scales from design (industrial-modernist)
findings.consequent: users feeling lost and anxious
findings.source: Curtain walls and machine precision do not help our wellbeing, p. 4
findings.quote: Present-day architectural culture eliminates the human scales from design... Without scaling information, users of those spaces feel lost and anxious.

findings.antecedent: industrial materials (glass, polished metal, concrete, bonded brick) with no texture, random surface patterns, and no nested hierarchy of mathematical scales
findings.consequent: users feeling lost and anxious
findings.source: Curtain walls and machine precision do not help our wellbeing, p. 4
findings.quote: Materials as used in industrial-modernism offer either no texture (e.g. glass and polished metal), or random surface patterns (e.g. concrete and bonded brick). The result is that there is no nested hierarchy of mathematical scales... Without scaling information, users of those spaces feel lost and anxious.

findings.antecedent: undifferentiated glass curtain wall (minimal/no internal frame, no subdivisions)
findings.consequent: anxiety rather than spatial experience that situates body via prehension
findings.source: Curtain walls and machine precision do not help our wellbeing, p. 4
findings.quote: Neurophysiology rules against the undifferentiated glass curtain wall. A large window made from plate glass with either minimal or no internal frame, nor any subdivisions, creates anxiety rather than a spatial experience that would situate our body via prehension.

findings.antecedent: older grilles/muntins between window panes and mullions between entire window units
findings.consequent: crucial psychological attachment of prehension
findings.source: Curtain walls and machine precision do not help our wellbeing, p. 4
findings.quote: The older grilles or muntins between window panes, and the mullions between entire window units provide the crucial psychological attachment of prehension; not the transparent glass.

findings.antecedent: successful bay windows (combining 'refuge' with 'prospect')
findings.consequent: reassuring spatial environment, visual connection to outside, object affordance on scale of entire body
findings.source: Curtain walls and machine precision do not help our wellbeing, p. 4
findings.quote: Another instance of object affordance occurs in traditional bay windows... Here, a reassuring spatial environment partially envelops one or more persons while connecting visually to the outside. Object affordance acts on the scale of the entire body. Using the vocabulary of biophilia, successful bay windows combine the two factors "refuge" with "prospect"...

findings.antecedent: glass curtain walls (offering no information, no protective psychological boundary)
findings.consequent: information and protective psychological boundary
findings.source: Curtain walls and machine precision do not help our wellbeing, p. 4
findings.quote: Do not confuse glass curtain walls (which offer no information, hence no protective psychological boundary) with the solid structural frame/grid that defines the spatial and visual boundary of bay windows (which give the cognitive experience of prehension). They have opposite effects.

findings.antecedent: solid structural frame/grid (defining spatial and visual boundary of bay windows)
findings.consequent: cognitive experience of prehension
findings.source: Curtain walls and machine precision do not help our wellbeing, p. 4
findings.quote: Do not confuse glass curtain walls (which offer no information, hence no protective psychological boundary) with the solid structural frame/grid that defines the spatial and visual boundary of bay windows (which give the cognitive experience of prehension). They have opposite effects.

findings.antecedent: basic neural modules ('primary' or 'primitive' brains) nested within more developed brain
findings.consequent: essential for basic life functions, automatic responses, and regulatory functions
findings.source: Architectural experience depends upon layers of complexity, p. 4
findings.quote: Every complex system has different layers of complexity built onto a core foundation. This is evident in evolved organs such as the brain, in which basic neural modules identified as "primary” or “primitive” brains are nested inside our own more developed one... Those evolutionary older portions are essential because our organism depends upon them for its basic life functions. The more evolutionary advanced layers that make us intelligent need those basic processing modules for automatic responses and regulatory functions.

findings.antecedent: primary elements of architectural form and space
findings.consequent: strongest influence on users, immediate visceral response to built form
findings.source: Journal of Architecture and Urbanism, p. 5
findings.quote: In a direct analogy, we can identify primary elements of architectural form and space that exert the strongest influence on users. Those elements trigger an immediate, visceral response to built form.

findings.antecedent: prevailing architectural culture (restricting architectural experience to 'style')
findings.consequent: negative adaptation
findings.source: Journal of Architecture and Urbanism, p. 5
findings.quote: But many people make the mistake of restricting architectural experience to the surface layer of several cognitively-nested layers of a complex informational system; namely, the layer corresponding to “style”. This reaction is learned from architectural culture. Less obvious yet primary (or primal) aspects of a building and space decide our predominant physiological and psychological responses; not style.

findings.antecedent: adaptive architecture (explicit organization of perceived complexity)
findings.consequent: positive interaction with neurophysiology developed for automatic information analysis
findings.source: Journal of Architecture and Urbanism, p. 5
findings.quote: Following the investigations of Christopher Alexander (2001, 2002, 2004, 2005), adaptive architecture relies upon the explicit organization of perceived complexity... The underlying assumption is that our neurophysiology developed for the purpose of analyzing information automatically.

findings.antecedent: traditional building forms (adapted to neurophysiology, using complex emotional feedback)
findings.consequent: feeling more at ease, boosted wellbeing
findings.source: Journal of Architecture and Urbanism, p. 5
findings.quote: Traditional building forms adapted to our neurophysiology so that we felt more at ease, as long as we built using complex emotional feedback as a guide... This is the reason why traditional buildings boost our wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: environmental information belonging to a special category we evolved to handle
findings.consequent: ability to process information positively
findings.source: Can we save money by eliminating information?, p. 5
findings.quote: We are constantly feeding on environmental information, but only if that information belongs to a special category that we evolved to handle. Otherwise, information (or lack of it) confuses us and makes us anxious.

findings.antecedent: highly sophisticated environmental complexity (either absent or overwhelming)
findings.consequent: anxiety (due to inability to process embedded information)
findings.source: Can we save money by eliminating information?, p. 5
findings.quote: If highly sophisticated environmental complexity is either absent, or it overwhelms us, this creates anxiety because we cannot process its embedded information to help us live.

findings.antecedent: design minimalism (removing information)
findings.consequent: structure utility or generic quality
findings.source: Can we save money by eliminating information?, p. 5
findings.quote: The commonly-heard justification linking design minimalism to utility turns out to be unfounded. Contrary to popular thinking, removing information does not make a structure more useful by making it more generic (Brand 1995).

findings.antecedent: stripping down a space (reducing information and substructure)
findings.consequent: utility for human participation, human qualities
findings.source: Can we save money by eliminating information?, p. 5
findings.quote: Stripping down a space actually reduces its utility for any use requiring human participation, leaving us with an industrial shed. It loses its human qualities.

findings.antecedent: generic International Style design
findings.consequent: psychologically healthy environment
findings.source: Can we save money by eliminating information?, p. 5
findings.quote: This reasoning rules out generic International Style design (triggering opposition from those who have bought into its supporting ideology).

findings.antecedent: non-visual components of sensory experiences (interpreting environment)
findings.consequent: how structures affect our body viscerally
findings.source: Including all of our other senses, p. 5
findings.quote: In The Eyes of the Skin, Juhani Pallasmaa (1996) discusses the non-visual components of sensory experiences interpreting our environment, which contribute to how structures affect our body viscerally.

findings.antecedent: conventional design pedagogy (ignoring non-visual environmental interactions, focusing on formal approaches/visual novelty)
findings.consequent: sensitivity to environmental interactions that trigger or reduce anxiety
findings.source: Including all of our other senses, p. 5-6
findings.quote: Instead of training architects to be sensitive to non-visual environmental interactions that either trigger or reduce anxiety, conventional design pedagogy ignores them, and focuses instead on formal approaches and visual novelty.

findings.antecedent: environmental stimuli (interpreted by sensory system, from all senses)
findings.consequent: physiological responses felt within entire body
findings.source: Past and future studies, p. 6
findings.quote: Environmental stimuli are constantly being interpreted by our sensory system, generating physiological responses felt within our entire body. This effect depends upon superimposed contributions coming from all of our senses.

findings.antecedent: complex character of interactions (from distinct mechanisms, different scales/ranges)
findings.consequent: changes with physical distance between human body and structure/surface
findings.source: Past and future studies, p. 6
findings.quote: Moreover, contributions from distinct mechanisms act on different scales and at different ranges. The complex character of these interactions changes with the physical distance between the human body and a structure or surface.

findings.antecedent: image-based design (ignoring mechanisms responsible for situatedness)
findings.consequent: details that define a welcoming environment (missing or incoherently juxtaposed)
findings.source: Past and future studies, p. 6
findings.quote: But “image-based design" ignores mechanisms responsible for situatedness. Details that define a welcoming environment are either missing, or are juxtaposed incoherently in many of today's buildings.

findings.antecedent: architects' focus on purity of abstract geometry
findings.consequent: ignored complex forces acting on body, sense of 'placelessness', anxiety
findings.source: Past and future studies, p. 6
findings.quote: Architects who focus on the purity of abstract geometry ignore the ensemble of complex forces acting on our body. The result leads to the opposite of situatedness: a sense of “placelessness”, and even anxiety.

findings.antecedent: abstract design (failing to evaluate/adjust for predictable human sensory reactions)
findings.consequent: threatening and oppressive environment when built
findings.source: Past and future studies, p. 6
findings.quote: An abstract design that looked fine in a rendering, but which failed to evaluate –and adjust for – all predictable human sensory reactions could turn out to be a threatening and oppressive environment when built.

findings.antecedent: users forced to use threatening/oppressive architectural spaces
findings.consequent: increased stress levels
findings.source: Past and future studies, p. 6
findings.quote: Users will avoid those architectural spaces, or force themselves to use them while fighting increased stress levels.

findings.antecedent: apparently benign design decisions based on abstractions
findings.consequent: negative physiological responses in the user
findings.source: Past and future studies, p. 6
findings.quote: Apparently benign design decisions based on abstractions can trigger negative physiological responses in the user.

findings.antecedent: space designed for a predetermined function/use (without considering visceral body reactions)
findings.consequent: dysfunctional or suitable for a totally different behavior
findings.source: Past and future studies, p. 6
findings.quote: A space designed for a predetermined function and use could be more suitable for a totally different behavior; or it could be dysfunctional, because our body is reacting viscerally to that space's hostile geometry, surfaces, details, and complexity (or lack of it) in an unexpected way.

findings.antecedent: adaptive approach to architecture and design (paying close attention to human evolution, following basic adaptive principles)
findings.consequent: users feeling situated in space, sense of belonging
findings.source: Conclusions, p. 6-7
findings.quote: A new, adaptive approach to architecture and design pays close attention to human evolution. Human beings respond to spaces, surfaces, detail, and ornament viscerally... Yet as long as the design has followed basic adaptive principles alluded to here, a user should feel situated in that space... evoke a “sense of belonging” that situates users.

findings.antecedent: built environment acquiring welcoming properties
findings.consequent: users feeling situated, sense of wonder (in exceptional cases)
findings.source: Journal of Architecture and Urbanism, p. 7
findings.quote: The built environment thus acquires welcoming properties. In exceptional cases, moreover, this perception could translate into a "sense of wonder", such as occurs in the great religious buildings of the past.

findings.antecedent: complex temporal system interacting seamlessly with complex spatial system
findings.consequent: adaptive, healing environments (better for health)
findings.source: Journal of Architecture and Urbanism, p. 7
findings.quote: We now possess the tools to create adaptive, healing environments that are better for our health. Those take us away from the practice of “architecture as image”.

limitations: Current architectural culture and practice often impede the application of neurophysiologically informed design principles, as architects are driven by style, fashion, inertia, money, and resistance to change (p. 3, p. 6).

There is a 'hidden bias within architectural culture' that prioritizes 'cult heroes' and 'image-based design' over scientific understanding of human responses, leading to 'psychologically unhealthy' buildings (p. 6).
Existing design pedagogy fails to teach sensitivity to non-visual environmental interactions that trigger or reduce anxiety, focusing instead on formal approaches and visual novelty (p. 5-6).
Architectural mistakes regarding human physiological responses have been ignored for too long (p. 6).
minimum_safe_summary: This paper argues for a fundamental human need for 'graspable handles' and other human-scaled, biologically adaptive features in the built environment, which are often absent in industrial-modernist architecture. It synthesizes research from neuroscience and psychology to propose that the absence of such features leads to psychological disconnection, stress, and anxiety, while their presence fosters wellbeing and a sense of situatedness. Key findings include that object affordance, fractal scaling, and a full spectrum of human scales are crucial for positive neurophysiological interactions, and that traditional architectures intuitively incorporated these elements. The paper critiques current architectural culture for prioritizing abstract aesthetics and style over human biological needs, leading to environments that are often psychologically detrimental.
